picks.title: Breath before toes
picks.from: Law 3, Let them discover the truth themselves (the forward-fold example, lines 90-94)
picks.stakes: Keep judging yourself by your toes and you pull harder, hold your breath, and decide yoga isn't for you.
picks.why_care: If you think you're 'too stiff for yoga', your breath is the one thing you can change on your first morning.
hooks: Can't touch your toes? Stop looking at your toes.
Your toes aren't the problem. Your breath is.

script.line: Can't touch your toes...? Stop looking at your toes... or one day you'll decide yoga isn't for you.
script.on_screen: Stop looking at your toes.

script.line: Try this with me. Fold forward and reach for your toes... a little more, gently. Now listen. Your breath got short... didn't it? When you fight your body, the breath goes first.
script.on_screen: Reach a little... and listen to your breath.

script.line: In Ashtanga, the breath comes first. The asana, the shape, comes second. Keep the breath long... and let your toes come when they come. So tomorrow... what will you watch? แล้วเจอกันครับ
script.on_screen: Breath first. Toes later. (small: See you)

caption: Can't touch your toes? Stop looking at them.

picks.title: What have you tried before?
picks.from: Law 2, Know what they came for vs. what they need (Boonchu application: 'What have you tried before?' then listen, lines 67-69), with the add-on step 'let them talk'
picks.habit: 9 Do it with others (a room and a teacher who notice when you're gone)
picks.stakes: Without someone who notices, the next thing you try ends like the last one: started, stopped, start again next year.
picks.why_care: Anyone with an app or a gym card they stopped using knows this feeling, and blames themselves for it.
hooks: The first thing I ask new students isn't about their body.
You didn't fail at yoga. Nobody noticed you stopped.

script.line: The first thing I ask a new student... isn't about their body.
script.on_screen: My first question isn't about your body.

script.line: I ask... what have you tried before? Because without that answer, this ends like the last one.
script.on_screen: What have you tried before?

script.line: Maybe you tried an app, a gym card, then a class in January. Started... then stopped. Then one busy week came, and it stopped again. And each time... you blamed yourself.
script.on_screen: Started. Stopped. Again and again.

script.line: But the tool was never the problem. Nobody noticed when you stopped. In a Mysore room, everyone practises at their own pace, same time every morning... and a teacher sees who isn't there. So what's on your list? แล้วเจอกันครับ

picks.title: Something is eating your time
picks.from: Gracián Maxim 7, 'Know how to withdraw' (line 256), used in Gracián's real meaning: cut what eats your time, not 'disappear so they miss you'
picks.stakes: Keep saying 'no time' and another year goes by with the same tired mornings, while the evening hours go to things you won't remember.
picks.why_care: Busy adults can't make more hours, but tonight they can choose one thing to stop.
hooks: You have time to practise. Something else is eating it.
No time to practise? Stop one thing tonight.

script.line: You have time to practise... Something else is eating it.
script.on_screen: Something is eating your time.

script.line: 'I have no time.' Say it every week... and a whole year goes by with the same tired mornings.
script.on_screen: 'I have no time.'

script.line: Gracián, a Spanish writer, saw this in 1647. He wrote... 'Know how to withdraw.' Step back, he meant... from the things that 'eat away precious time.' For me, it was [BOONCHU: the one thing you stopped doing at night so you could practise early].
script.on_screen: '...eat away precious time.' Gracián, 1647

script.line: So don't look for more time. Stop one thing tonight, and go to bed a little earlier. The morning is yours again. What will you stop? แล้วเจอกันครับ
script.on_screen: Stop one thing tonight. (small: See you)

caption: You have time to practise. Something else is eating it.

Gracián, 1647' (the words that carry the meaning, so it can't read as 'know when to quit' with the sound off).
picks.risk: Use only Gracián's real meaning (step back from what eats your time), never the note's 'disappear' gloss; Boonchu fills the [BOONCHU] line with one short true sentence or the beat is cut; no promise about sleep. picks.title: Day one: this will be hard
picks.from: Pledge line 'Tell the truth about what Ashtanga can and cannot do' (line 352), with the day-one honesty line (line 338) and the direction.md flip 'Hard for 2 weeks'
picks.habit: 2 Get stronger (body-weight strength built by coming back)
picks.stakes: If nobody warns you, the first shaky, sore week feels like proof you're not made for this, and you quit.
picks.why_care: Knowing the hard part is normal and short turns 'I'm not made for this' into 'this is only week one'.
hooks: Day one, I tell new students: this will be hard.

script.line: Nobody warns you... so you think you failed. Your arms will shake in chaturanga, the low push-up. Your legs will too. Hard for about two weeks... and then the hard part changes. The hard part becomes... coming back.

picks.title: Nobody claps in a Mysore room
picks.from: Gracián Maxim 1, 'Be common in nothing' (line 238), used in Gracián's real meaning: don't live for the crowd's taste
picks.habit: 6 Calm the mind (90 minutes, no phone, no audience)
picks.stakes: A practice that runs on likes and claps stops the day the claps stop.
picks.why_care: Serious practitioners post their practice too, and this asks who the morning is really for, without blaming anyone.
hooks: Nobody claps in a Mysore room. That's the point.
Practise for the likes, and you'll stop when they stop.

script.line: Nobody claps in a Mysore room... and that's the point.

script.line: If you practise for the likes... you'll stop when the likes stop.

script.line: Gracián, a Spanish writer, put it in three words in 1647. 'Common in nothing.' He meant... don't live for the crowd's taste. I post Reels too. But this isn't my practice. My practice is tomorrow at [BOONCHU: your real practice time]... with nobody watching.
script.on_screen: 'Common in nothing.' Gracián, 1647

picks.title: Your best lesson plan
picks.from: Law 1, Credibility is non-negotiable (the Carnegie quote, line 28), with Maxim 9 in our own words: only teach what you practise
picks.habit: 10 Go traditional (a method passed teacher to student, by a teacher who still practises)
picks.stakes: A teacher who skips their own mat slowly teaches from memory, not from a practice they still live.
picks.why_care: For a busy teacher, their own practice is the easiest thing to drop, and it's where everything they say in class comes from.
hooks: Your best lesson plan is your own practice.
Skip your own mat, and you teach from memory.

script.line: Your best lesson plan... is your own practice.

script.line: Your own mat is the easiest thing to skip. Skip it long enough... and you teach from memory.
script.on_screen: Skip your mat. Teach from memory.

script.line: A book from 1915, The Art of Public Speaking, said it plainly. 'Public speaking is public utterance, public issuance, of the man himself.' What you teach... is you, out loud. [BOONCHU: one true moment when your own practice changed how you teach an asana].

script.line: Before you teach tomorrow... get on your own mat first. I've done it six days a week since 2008... and I still need it. When did you last practise just for you? แล้วเจอกันครับ

picks.title: The quiet after a correction
picks.from: Law 5, Rhythm and rest, with Carnegie's rule 'On Pause and Power' (lines 284-287), in our own words
picks.habit: 8 Mind-body movement (the body learns in the quiet breath after a correction)
picks.stakes: Correct and keep talking, and the student never gets the quiet breaths to feel the change, so the same correction comes back tomorrow.
picks.why_care: Practitioners who wonder why a correction 'doesn't stick', and teachers who fill every silence, meet this every morning.
hooks: After I correct you, I stop talking. On purpose.
The correction takes one second. The learning comes after.

script.line: (quiet voice-over) After I correct you... I stop talking. On purpose.
script.on_screen: After the correction, I stop talking.

script.line: One small word from me. Then I step back... (one breath, about 5 s: no voice, only the breath of the room, 'Then I wait.' on screen) ...Keep talking, and you never feel what changed.
script.on_screen: Then I wait. Your body answers.

picks.title: Notice who's missing
picks.from: Stage 3, Connection (lines 184-194: see each person, remember, every morning), with the Law 5 fix 'notice who is missing, say See you tomorrow?'
picks.habit: 9 Do it with others (a room where someone notices when you're gone)
picks.stakes: A teacher who doesn't notice the empty mat loses that student quietly and never learns why.
picks.why_care: Every teacher has had a regular stop coming without a word, and noticing is a skill they can start practising tomorrow morning.
hooks: The hardest skill in teaching? Noticing who's missing.
